uncited: SDF Rotation applies a rotational transformation to a signed distance field primitive by rotating the query point inversely before evaluating the base distance function.

Unlike [SDF Translation](5820-sdf-translation.md), which uses vector subtraction to position a primitive, rotation applies an inverse rotation matrix or quaternion to the sampling point, allowing the primitive to be oriented arbitrarily in world space without modifying its internal geometric definition.
Stored as the second field of the Rotation struct.
- Non-unit quaternions: If the stored quaternion is not normalized, the inverse rotation will scale the point incorrectly.
- Precision errors: Repeated rotations can accumulate floating-point errors.
- Time complexity: $O(1)$ per query, dominated by quaternion multiplication (constant number of arithmetic operations).
- Memory complexity: $O(1)$ additional memory for the inverse quaternion calculation.
- Strengths: Efficient orientation of primitives without modifying the base SDF code; supports arbitrary rotations via quaternions.
- Limitations: Requires careful handling of quaternion normalization; slightly more expensive than translation due to quaternion multiplication overhead.
- When to use: When primitives need to be oriented at arbitrary angles in the scene.
- When not to use: When performance is critical and only axis-aligned rotations are needed (matrix multiplication might be faster on some hardware).
SDF rotation is a fundamental technique in ray marching and procedural geometry, enabling the creation of complex scenes from simple primitives.
It builds on the concept of transforming the query point rather than the geometry itself, a principle shared with [SDF Translation](5820-sdf-translation.md) and [SDF Scaling](5818-sdf-scaling.md).
The method is widely used in real-time graphics for its efficiency and simplicity.
